questions.title: Variable Types and Memory Placement
questions.question: Declare a static variable, an instance variable, and a local variable within a single Java class, instantiate the class, and print all three values to illustrate their distinct scopes.
questions.explanation: Java defines three primary categories of variables based on their declaration context: static variables, instance variables, and local variables. Static (class) variables are declared with the static modifier within a class body; they are created when the class is loaded into the JVM Metaspace and shared among all instances. Instance variables are declared in a class without static; they are allocated on the Java heap whenever a new object is created and exist as long as the object is reachable. Local variables are declared inside methods, constructors, or blocks; they reside in the thread's call stack frame and exist only for the duration of that block. This exercise demonstrates how to access static variables via class or instance qualification, instance variables through an instantiated object reference, and local variables directly within their enclosing method scope.
hints: Declare 'static int staticVar' directly inside the class body.
Declare 'int instanceVar' directly inside the class body without the static keyword.
Declare 'int localVar' inside the main method body and instantiate the class to access 'instanceVar'.
questions.expectedOutput:
Static variable: 100
Instance variable: 50
Local variable: 10

questions.title: Default Field Value Initialization
questions.question: Print the automatic default initialization values assigned by the JVM to uninitialized instance fields for all eight primitive types and an object reference type (`String`).
questions.explanation: In Java, instance and static member fields are guaranteed to be initialized with default values by the JVM during object allocation and class initialization (JLS §4.12.5). When memory is allocated on the heap for an object, the runtime zeroes out the memory block prior to running constructors. Consequently, byte, short, int, and long fields default to 0; float and double default to +0.0f and +0.0d; char defaults to the null character '\u0000' (numeric value 0); boolean fields default to false; and all reference types (including String, arrays, and custom classes) default to null. Local variables, by contrast, reside on the thread stack and do not receive automatic default values; attempting to read an uninitialized local variable results in a compile-time error.
hints: Declare uninitialized member fields for byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean, and String.
Instantiate the class in the main entry method to access these instance fields.
Print the char field alongside its integer cast ((int) defaultChar) to clearly display '\u0000' as numerical 0.
questions.expectedOutput:
byte: 0
short: 0
int: 0
long: 0
float: 0.0
double: 0.0
char: [] (code: 0)
boolean: false
reference: null

questions.title: Block and Iteration Scope Boundaries
questions.question: Demonstrate lexical block scope by declaring a variable inside an `if` block and another inside a `for` loop, then contrast this with accumulating results into an outer scoped variable that outlives the loop.
questions.explanation: Java enforces strict lexical block scoping delimited by curly braces ({ ... }). Any variable declared inside a block—such as an if-statement body or the initialization header of a for-loop—has a lifetime and visibility confined strictly to that block. Once the instruction pointer exits the closing brace, the variable's stack slot is deallocated or invalidated, and any attempt to reference it from outer code causes a compile-time symbol resolution error. To persist values computed inside conditional branches or loops across iterations or beyond the loop's conclusion, the accumulator variable must be declared in an outer enclosing scope before the block is entered.
hints: Declare a variable inside 'if (true) { ... }' and print it strictly within that block.
Use a loop 'for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++)' and observe that 'i' is unreachable after the loop.
Declare an outer accumulator 'int sum = 0;' before the loop and print it after the loop finishes.
questions.expectedOutput:
Inside if-block: blockScoped = 42
Iteration 1: iterationScoped = 10
Iteration 2: iterationScoped = 20
Iteration 3: iterationScoped = 30
After loop: outerAccumulator = 60

questions.title: Compile-Time Constants with Final Modifier
questions.question: Use a `final` local variable `PI` to calculate the area of a circle with radius `5.0`, and explain how the `final` modifier prevents reassignment.
questions.explanation: The final keyword in Java establishes an immutability constraint on a variable's binding. When applied to a local variable or field, final mandates that the variable can be assigned a value exactly once. Once assigned, any subsequent assignment attempt causes javac to throw a compilation error: 'cannot assign a value to final variable'. When a final primitive variable is initialized with a constant expression (e.g., final double PI = 3.141592653589793), the Java compiler treats it as a compile-time constant, inlining the raw literal directly into the generated bytecode instructions. This exercise shows how final ensures mathematical invariants remain untouched during algorithmic calculations.
hints: Declare 'final double PI = 3.141592653589793;' to create an unchangeable local constant.
Compute the area using 'PI * radius * radius'.
Observe that attempting 'PI = 3.14;' after initialization triggers a compile-time error.

questions.title: Multiple Declarations and Expression Evaluation
questions.question: Declare multiple variables of the same type within a single statement (`int a = 5, b = 10, c;`), compute `c = a + b`, and print the resulting values.
questions.explanation: Java allows multiple variables of the same data type to be declared in a single comma-separated statement (JLS §14.4). In the declaration int a = 5, b = 10, c;, variables a and b are both declared and immediately initialized with integer literals, whereas c is declared without an initial value. Because c is a local variable residing on the thread stack frame, it does not receive a default value. However, before c is read in any subsequent expression, it is assigned the result of a + b, satisfying the compiler's strict definite assignment rules. While convenient for concise examples, declaring one variable per line is generally preferred in enterprise development for clearer code reviews and Git diff tracking.
hints: Combine declarations using commas: 'int a = 5, b = 10, c;'.
Assign 'c = a + b;' before reading or printing 'c'.
Print all three variables to confirm successful assignment and calculation.

questions.title: Default Field Value Display
questions.question: Create a class declaring uninitialized instance variables of types `boolean`, `byte`, `int`, `double`, `char`, and `Object`. Print their automatic default values.
questions.explanation: This exercise reinforces the zero-initialization semantics of Java instance fields across different type families. Whenever a new instance of a class is allocated on the heap, the Java Virtual Machine guarantees that all instance fields are initialized to default values before constructors or initialization blocks execute. Integral types (byte, short, int, long) default to 0; floating-point types (float, double) default to 0.0; char defaults to the null code point '\u0000'; boolean fields default to false; and reference types (like Object) default to null. This automatic zeroing prevents unpredictable values from uninitialized memory, guaranteeing deterministic state across JVM implementations.
hints: Declare uninitialized member fields: 'boolean flag;', 'byte b;', 'int i;', 'double d;', 'char c;', 'Object obj;'.
Instantiate the class inside main: 'Solution instance = new Solution();'.
Cast the char field to an integer ((int) c) so the null character '\u0000' prints as numerical 0.
questions.expectedOutput:
boolean: false
byte: 0
int: 0
double: 0.0
char: [] (code: 0)
Object: null

questions.title: Shadowing Demonstration and Fix
questions.question: Write a class with an instance variable `value`. In a setter method, declare a parameter also named `value`. Show how to resolve the collision using `this`.
questions.explanation: Variable shadowing occurs when a variable declared within an inner scope (such as a method parameter or local variable) shares the exact same identifier as a variable in an outer enclosing scope (such as an instance field). In Java, local identifiers take precedence over field identifiers. Writing value = value inside a setter merely assigns the parameter to itself, leaving the instance field unchanged. To bypass this shadowing and explicitly reference the instance field on the current object heap memory, the code must qualify the identifier with the this keyword (this.value = value). This is the universal idiom in Java constructors, setters, and builder patterns.
hints: Declare a private instance field: 'private int value;'.
In setValue(int value), write 'this.value = value;' to assign the parameter to the instance field.
Print the field before and after invoking the setter to verify that the value was updated.
questions.expectedOutput:
Initial value: 10
Updated value: 42

questions.title: Local Variable Definite Assignment
questions.question: Write a method demonstrating that local variables do not receive default values and must be explicitly initialized before reading, handling conditional branching assignment.
questions.explanation: Under the Java Language Specification (JLS §16), the compiler enforces strict 'definite assignment' rules for all local variables. Unlike instance and static fields, which receive automatic zero-initialization, a local variable allocated on a thread stack frame contains arbitrary uninitialized data. The compiler performs static data-flow analysis to ensure that every possible execution path assigns a value to a local variable before that variable is read. If an if-statement initializes a variable inside the if branch but omits the else branch, the compiler marks the variable as potentially unassigned and halts with a compile-time error. Providing exhaustive initialization across all branches satisfies definite assignment.
hints: Declare 'int result;' without initializing it immediately.
Use an if-else structure ensuring that BOTH branches assign a concrete value to 'result'.
Observe that omitting the 'else' branch causes javac to fail with 'variable result might not have been initialized'.
questions.expectedOutput:
Score: 85
Bonus awarded: 15
Total: 100

questions.title: Block Scope Isolation
questions.question: Write nested code blocks `{}` inside a method showing that a variable declared in an inner block cannot be accessed once that block exits.
questions.explanation: Java supports standalone block statements delimited by curly braces ({ ... }) inside method bodies. Each block defines an isolated lexical scope and introduces a nested scope frame in the compiler's symbol table. Variables declared within an inner block are visible to that block and any child blocks nested inside it. However, once the closing curly brace of that block is reached, those variables go out of scope and become inaccessible to subsequent code in the outer block. Furthermore, Java prohibits variable shadowing between nested local scopes: declaring a local variable with the same name as an active variable in an enclosing local block triggers a compile-time error.
hints: Declare 'int outerVar = 10;' in the method.
Open a standalone block '{ int innerVar = 20; ... }' and print both variables inside it.
Print 'outerVar' after the block closes, noting that 'innerVar' cannot be accessed outside.
questions.expectedOutput:
Outer scope: outerVar = 10
Inner block: outerVar = 10, innerVar = 20
Back in outer scope: outerVar = 10

questions.title: Type Inference with var
questions.question: Refactor verbose declarations (such as generic collections and maps) using the `var` keyword for local variable type inference, and document contexts where `var` cannot be used.
questions.explanation: Introduced in Java 10 (JEP 286), the var keyword provides local variable type inference, allowing developers to omit explicit type declarations when the type can be unambiguously inferred from the initializer expression. Unlike dynamic languages (e.g., Python or JavaScript), var does not make Java dynamically typed; the compiler infers the exact static type at compile time and encodes it directly into the generated bytecode. var is restricted to local variables with initializers, enhanced for-loop headers, and index loop headers. It cannot be used for member fields, method return types, method parameters, uninitialized variables, null assignments, or lambda expressions lacking explicit target types.
hints: Use 'var list = new ArrayList<String>();' to replace verbose collection declarations.
Use 'var map = new HashMap<String, Integer>();' and populate it with sample entries.
Add comments explaining that 'var' is illegal for class fields, method parameters, and uninitialized locals.
questions.expectedOutput:
Total users (inferred int): 2
Top user (inferred String): Alice
Score (inferred Map): 95

questions.title: Static Instance Tracking Across Instantiations
questions.question: Implement an object tracking mechanism in a class that increments a `static` counter inside its constructor, and verify that the count updates consistently as new objects are instantiated.
questions.explanation: Because static variables belong to the class rather than any single instance, all instantiated objects share the exact same memory location for that field in the JVM Metaspace/Heap. By placing an increment operation (instanceCount++) inside a class constructor, every invocation of new increments this shared counter. Each individual instance can also store its own unique sequential ID by capturing the counter value during construction. This demonstrates the distinction between class-level shared state and individual instance state, a fundamental design pattern for object pooling, factory tracking, and unique ID generation.
hints: Declare a 'private static int instanceCount = 0;' class variable.
In the constructor, assign 'this.id = ++instanceCount;' to give each instance a unique ID.
Instantiate three objects and print their individual IDs alongside the final static count.
questions.expectedOutput:
Item A ID: 1
Item B ID: 2
Item C ID: 3
Total objects created: 3

questions.title: Parameter Shadowing and Field Disambiguation
questions.question: Create a class where a method's local variable and parameter shadow an instance field, and use the `this` reference to inspect both the shadowed field and local variables within the same method.
questions.explanation: This exercise explores lexical scope resolution and name hiding in Java. When a local variable or method parameter shares an identifier with an instance field, the compiler resolves unqualified references to the innermost declaration (the parameter or local variable). This hides (shadows) the instance field from simple name resolution. To access the shadowed instance field, the code must explicitly qualify the reference using this.fieldName. Understanding this disambiguation is crucial for avoiding silent logic bugs where a parameter is inadvertently assigned to itself instead of updating instance state.
hints: Declare an instance field: 'int data = 100;'.
In a method updateData(int data), declare a local variable or parameter that shares the identifier 'data'.
Print 'data' to display the local value and 'this.data' to display the instance field value.
questions.expectedOutput:
Parameter 'data': 500
Instance field 'this.data': 100
Updated instance field 'this.data': 500

questions.title: State Isolation: Static versus Instance Variables
questions.question: Instantiate two independent objects of a class and demonstrate that mutating an instance variable affects only that specific object, whereas mutating a static variable modifies shared state across both objects.
questions.explanation: The core architectural distinction between instance and static fields lies in memory allocation and state isolation. Every instance of a class allocated on the heap receives its own distinct memory block for its instance fields; modifying an instance field on object A has no effect on object B. In contrast, a static variable exists as a single memory slot associated with the Class object in the JVM. Both object A and object B reference this same shared location. Modifying the static variable through either reference (or directly via the class name) updates the value seen across all instances.
hints: Declare 'int instanceCount = 0;' and 'static int sharedCount = 0;' inside a Counter class.
Create two instances: 'Counter c1 = new Counter();' and 'Counter c2 = new Counter();'.
Increment c1's instance variable and increment the shared static variable, then print values from both instances.
questions.expectedOutput:
After c1 increments twice:
c1.instanceVal: 2, c1.staticVal: 2
c2.instanceVal: 0, c2.staticVal: 2

questions.title: Blank Final Field Initialization Across Constructors
questions.question: Implement a class with a blank final instance field and demonstrate that every constructor must initialize it exactly once, supporting different constructor parameter paths.
questions.explanation: A blank final field is a final instance variable that is declared without an immediate inline initializer. According to JLS §8.3.1.2, a blank final instance field must be definitely assigned by the end of every constructor in the class; otherwise, a compile-time error occurs. Once assigned during object construction, the field's value cannot be altered for the remaining lifetime of that object. This pattern is essential for creating immutable value objects and domain entities whose final configuration parameters vary based on which constructor overload is invoked.
hints: Declare 'private final int threshold;' without an inline value.
Provide a default constructor that sets 'this.threshold = 100;' and a parameterized constructor that sets 'this.threshold = customValue;'.
Instantiate objects using both constructors and print their configured thresholds.
questions.expectedOutput:
Policy: DEFAULT | Limit: 100
Policy: ENTERPRISE | Limit: 500

questions.title: Static and Instance Initialization Block Execution Order
questions.question: Write a class containing both static and instance initialization blocks alongside a constructor, and print diagnostic messages to demonstrate the exact execution order across multiple object instantiations.
questions.explanation: The Java Virtual Machine follows a strict initialization sequence when classes are loaded and instantiated. Static initialization blocks (static { ... }) execute exactly once when the class is first loaded by the ClassLoader, prior to any object creation or static method invocation. In contrast, instance initialization blocks ({ ... }) execute every time a new instance is created via new. The instance block runs immediately after the superclass constructor completes and right before the body of the class's own constructor executes. Creating a second instance runs the instance block and constructor again, but skips the static block entirely.
hints: Declare a 'static { ... }' block that prints a static init message.
Declare an instance initializer block '{ ... }' that prints an instance init message.
Instantiate two objects in main and observe that the static block runs only once.
questions.expectedOutput:
Creating first instance:
[1] Static initializer block executed (class loaded)
[2] Instance initializer block executed
[3] Constructor executed
Creating second instance:
[2] Instance initializer block executed
[3] Constructor executed

questions.title: Order of Initialization Tracker
questions.question: Write a class combining static blocks, instance initialization blocks, static variables, instance variables, and constructors. Print output from each to prove the exact execution order.
questions.explanation: This exercise traces the complete initialization order of a Java class. Static variable initializers and static blocks execute first in their textual order of appearance when the class is loaded. When an object is instantiated, instance variable initializers and instance initializer blocks execute next, also in their textual order of appearance. Finally, the constructor body executes. Tracking this lifecycle is essential for understanding when dependent resources (such as database connection pools or configured logger instances) become safely available for use.
hints: Initialize a static variable using a helper method that logs its execution.
Initialize an instance variable using a helper method that logs its execution.
Place print statements in the static block, instance block, and constructor to observe the full sequence.

Step 1: Static variable initialized
Step 2: Static block executed
Main method started
Step 3: Instance variable initialized
Step 4: Instance block executed
Step 5: Constructor executed

questions.title: Final Variable Reassignment Trap
questions.question: Demonstrate the behavior of `final` applied to primitive types versus reference types. Show that a `final` object reference cannot be reassigned, but its internal fields can be mutated.
questions.explanation: A common point of confusion in Java is the distinction between a constant reference and an immutable object. When a primitive variable is declared final, its actual numeric value cannot be changed. However, when an object reference is declared final, the immutability constraint applies strictly to the reference address stored in the variable; the variable cannot be reassigned to point to a different object on the heap (ref = new Object() causes a compile-time error). Crucially, the final modifier does not make the referenced object's internal fields immutable. Unless the object's class is designed to be immutable, its internal fields can be freely modified through the final reference.
hints: Declare a final StringBuilder: 'final StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("Initial");'.
Mutate it via 'sb.append(" Mutated");' and show that mutation succeeds.
Observe that attempting 'sb = new StringBuilder();' triggers a compile-time reassignment error.
questions.expectedOutput:
Initial box content: 50
Mutated box content: 99
Primitive constant: 100

questions.title: Variable Lifetime in Loops
questions.question: Write a loop creating objects. Track whether a reference inside the loop body persists across iterations or goes out of scope on each loop cycle.
questions.explanation: Variables declared inside a loop body have a scope and lifetime confined to a single iteration. On each iteration of the loop, a new local variable is allocated in the thread's stack frame. When the loop body completes that iteration, the local reference goes out of scope. If the object created during that iteration was not assigned to an external collection or outer reference, it becomes unreachable and eligible for garbage collection. This exercise demonstrates how declaring temporary objects inside loop bodies avoids leaking state between iterations.
hints: Declare a local object reference inside the loop body: 'for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { Sample obj = new Sample(i); ... }'.
Print the object's state inside the loop to confirm it is newly instantiated on each iteration.
Observe that 'obj' is not accessible outside the loop block.
questions.expectedOutput:
Iteration 1: Payload object ID = 1
Iteration 2: Payload object ID = 2
Iteration 3: Payload object ID = 3
Loop finished. Loop-scoped variables successfully deallocated.

questions.title: Static vs Instance Isolation
questions.question: Create a `Counter` class where multiple instances modify both an instance variable `count` and a static variable `globalCount`. Verify data isolation and sharing.
questions.explanation: This exercise contrasts per-instance state isolation with shared class-level state. When an instance method increments both an instance field and a static field, the instance field increment updates only that specific object's memory on the heap. The static field increment, however, updates the shared counter in the Class object. By creating two distinct Counter instances and invoking operations on them independently, students observe that instance counts remain isolated while the static global count accumulates changes from all instances.
hints: Define an instance field 'int count = 0;' and a static field 'static int globalCount = 0;'.
Implement an increment() method that updates both fields.
Call increment() on instance A twice and on instance B once, then inspect both objects' states.
questions.expectedOutput:
Counter A instance count: 2
Counter B instance count: 1
Shared global count: 3

questions.title: Blank Final Field Initialization
questions.question: Create a class with blank final instance fields. Ensure all constructors initialize them under different parameter paths, preventing compilation errors.
questions.explanation: Blank final instance fields must be explicitly initialized in every constructor of a class (unless one constructor delegates to another using this(...)). The Java compiler performs static analysis to verify that every path through every constructor assigns a value to each blank final field exactly once. If a constructor contains an execution branch (e.g., an if-else statement) where a blank final field might not be assigned, the compiler raises a 'variable might not have been initialized' error. Once assigned in the constructor, the field becomes permanently read-only for that instance.
hints: Declare 'private final String serviceUrl;' and 'private final int timeoutMs;' without inline values.

questions.title: Lambda Scope and Effectively Final Variables
questions.question: Demonstrate the 'effectively final' rule for local variables captured by a lambda expression, and show how to mutate shared state from inside a lambda using a single-element array or an `AtomicInteger`.
questions.explanation: When a lambda expression or anonymous inner class references a local variable from an enclosing method, Java requires that variable to be final or effectively final (JLS §6.5.6.1). A variable is effectively final if its value is never modified after initialization. This restriction exists because the lambda captures a copy of the variable's value on the heap; allowing local primitives to be modified inside the lambda would lead to inconsistencies between the thread's stack and the lambda's captured copy. To safely mutate state from within a lambda, developers use a wrapper object whose reference remains effectively final while its contents change, such as a single-element array (int[] count = {0}) or an AtomicInteger.
hints: Declare an effectively final primitive 'int factor = 2;' used read-only inside the lambda.
Use 'AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger(0);' to allow mutation from inside the lambda.

Array box value: 10

questions.title: Two-Class Inheritance Initialization Chain
questions.question: Create parent and child classes each containing static initialization blocks, instance initialization blocks, and constructors, and print the exact sequence of initialization events when calling `new Child()`.
questions.explanation: In an inheritance hierarchy, class initialization and object construction follow a strict multi-phase sequence across parent and child classes. First, all static blocks execute from top to bottom down the inheritance chain: the superclass static block runs before the subclass static block. Second, when an instance of the subclass is created, object construction proceeds hierarchically: the superclass instance initializer blocks execute, followed by the superclass constructor body. Once the superclass constructor completes, the subclass instance initializer blocks execute, and finally the subclass constructor body runs. Understanding this hierarchy prevents subtle initialization order bugs where subclass state is accessed before it has been initialized.
hints: Define Parent with a static block, an instance block, and a constructor.
Define Child extending Parent with its own static block, instance block, and constructor.
Instantiate new Child() in main and observe the interleaved execution order.
questions.expectedOutput:
Calling new Child():
[1] Parent static block
[2] Child static block
[3] Parent instance block
[4] Parent constructor
[5] Child instance block
[6] Child constructor

questions.title: Stack Frame Variable Isolation in Recursion
questions.question: Write a recursive factorial method that prints the memory identity or call depth of its local parameter on each invocation to demonstrate that each recursive call operates on an independent stack frame.
questions.explanation: Every method invocation in Java allocates a new stack frame on the calling thread's call stack. A stack frame contains the method's local variable table, operand stack, and frame data. When a method invokes itself recursively, each nested invocation receives its own independent stack frame with its own copies of parameters and local variables. Modifying a parameter or local variable in a deeper recursive frame has no effect on the local variables of earlier frames higher up the stack. When a frame finishes executing, it is popped off the stack, and execution resumes in the caller's frame with its local variables preserved.
hints: In factorial(int n), declare a local variable 'int currentVal = n;'.
Print 'currentVal' on the way down into the recursion and on the way back up.
Return 1 when n <= 1 to terminate the recursion cleanly.

Entering frame: n = 3
Entering frame: n = 2
Entering frame: n = 1
Base case reached: returning 1
Exiting frame: n = 2, returned = 2
Exiting frame: n = 3, returned = 6
Final Factorial(3): 6

questions.title: Shared Static State Race Conditions and Synchronization
questions.question: Demonstrate a race condition where multiple concurrent threads modify an unsynchronized shared static variable, then resolve the issue using `AtomicInteger`.
questions.explanation: Because static variables reside in shared memory accessible by all threads, concurrently modifying a plain static variable (such as counter++) introduces a race condition. The increment operation is not atomic; it consists of three distinct bytecode steps: reading the variable from main memory, incrementing it in a thread-local CPU register, and writing the result back to main memory. When two threads interleave these steps, increments are lost. Using java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger solves this without explicit lock synchronization by using hardware-level Compare-And-Swap (CAS) instructions to guarantee thread-safe atomic updates.
hints: Spawn two threads that each loop 10,000 times incrementing an AtomicInteger.
Call thread.join() on both threads to ensure they finish before reading the result.
Compare the deterministic AtomicInteger result against the theoretical total.
questions.expectedOutput: Final synchronized count: 2000

questions.title: Thread-Safe Lazy Singleton Implementation
questions.question: Implement a thread-safe lazy Singleton using double-checked locking with a `volatile` static reference, and verify that multiple calls return the exact same instance.
questions.explanation: Lazy initialization delays creating an object until it is first requested. In multithreaded environments, a naive lazy singleton implementation (if (instance == null) instance = new Singleton()) can lead to race conditions where multiple threads create separate instances. Double-checked locking solves this efficiently by checking if the instance is null before acquiring a synchronized lock, avoiding synchronization overhead on subsequent calls. The static instance variable must be marked volatile to prevent CPU and compiler instruction reordering, ensuring other threads do not observe a partially constructed object.
hints: Declare 'private static volatile Singleton instance;' to prevent instruction reordering.
Check 'if (instance == null)' before entering the synchronized block, then check again inside.
Verify that two calls to getInstance() return identical references using the '==' operator.

Singleton constructor invoked
s1 == s2: true

questions.title: Lazy Initializer Pattern
questions.question: Implement a thread-safe lazy-initialization holder idiom for a costly resource object without using synchronization blocks.
questions.explanation: The Initialization-on-Demand Holder idiom (also known as the Bill Pugh Singleton) provides thread-safe lazy initialization without the performance overhead or complexity of synchronized blocks or double-checked locking. It relies on the JVM's class initialization phase guaranteed by the Java Language Specification (JLS §12.4.2). The outer class can be loaded without initializing the costly resource. The nested static holder class is loaded only when its static member is explicitly referenced by getInstance(). The JVM guarantees that static class initialization is completely thread-safe, providing clean, zero-overhead lazy loading.

Make the outer class constructor private.
Implement 'getInstance()' returning 'Holder.INSTANCE'.

r1 == r2: true

questions.title: Inheritance Initialization Hierarchy

questions.explanation: Extending inheritance across three generations reveals the full initialization order enforced by the JVM. When new Child() is called, class loading triggers the execution of all static blocks in descending order from the top of the inheritance chain: GrandParent static, Parent static, and finally Child static. After class loading completes, object instantiation proceeds generation by generation: GrandParent instance blocks and constructor execute first, followed by Parent instance blocks and constructor, and finally Child instance blocks and constructor. Understanding this hierarchy is essential for designing robust object frameworks and preventing initialization errors in subclassed components.

questions.title: Forward Reference Detection
questions.question: Write a sample showing illegal forward references in class variable initializers and implement the necessary code reorganization to resolve the dependencies.
questions.explanation: Under JLS §8.3.3, a member variable initialization cannot make a simple forward reference to a variable declared later in the class text. For example, declaring static int a = b + 1; followed by static int b = 10; causes javac to fail with 'illegal forward reference'. This restriction prevents reading uninitialized memory during the linear execution of class initializers. Reordering the declarations so that dependencies appear before their consumers resolves the issue. Interestingly, qualifying the forward reference (e.g., Solution.b) bypasses the compiler error but reads the default value 0 instead of the unassigned value 10, highlighting why textual ordering is critical.
hints: Demonstrate the resolved order where dependent variables are declared after their inputs.
Explain that reading an uninitialized static variable via class qualification returns default 0.
Print the properly initialized dependent variables.
questions.expectedOutput:

questions.title: Scope-Aware Symbol Table
questions.question: Write a simple program that simulates a compiler's symbol table: push new scopes on `{`, register variable names, search current and parent scopes, and pop on `}`.
questions.explanation: Compilers manage variable scope using a data structure called a Symbol Table. A classic implementation uses a stack of maps (or a cactus stack). When the compiler encounters an opening curly brace ({), it pushes a new scope (Map<String, String>) onto the scope stack. Variable declarations inside that block are registered in the active scope map. When looking up an identifier, the compiler searches from the current scope upward through parent scopes to the global scope. When the closing curly brace (}) is encountered, the current scope is popped off the stack, removing its local variables from scope.
hints: Use a 'Deque<Map<String, String>>' to represent the scope stack.
In enterScope(), push a new HashMap onto the deque; in exitScope(), pop the top map.
In lookup(name), iterate from the top of the stack down to find the closest visible definition.
questions.expectedOutput:
Inside block - localVar: String
Inside block - globalVar: int
After block - localVar: null
After block - globalVar: int

questions.title: Thread-Local Scoped Storage
questions.question: Implement a transaction manager using `ThreadLocal<T>` that provides isolated execution context variables across different threads without leakage.
questions.explanation: Java's java.lang.ThreadLocal provides thread-scoped variable storage. Each thread accessing a ThreadLocal instance maintains an independent, isolated copy of the variable inside its own Thread.threadLocals map. This eliminates the need for synchronization when managing per-thread state, such as transaction IDs, security tokens, or database sessions. Because thread pools (e.g., ExecutorService) reuse threads across requests, failing to call threadLocal.remove() can cause data leakage between unrelated requests and prevent objects from being garbage collected. Proper design requires wrapping ThreadLocal usage in try-finally blocks to guarantee cleanup.
hints: Declare a 'private static final ThreadLocal<String> transactionId = new ThreadLocal<>();'.
Set the transaction ID in worker threads and verify that each thread reads only its own value.
Always call 'transactionId.remove()' in a finally block to prevent memory leaks in thread pools.
questions.expectedOutput:
Thread 1 context: TXN-1001
Thread 2 context: TXN-2002
Main thread context: null
